newsitem.title: KENYA: Kenyan forces struggle to contain violence.
newsitem.headline: Kenyan forces struggle to contain violence.

text.p: Security forces were struggling to halt civil violence which has claimed 31 lives in the major Kenyan port of Mombasa in the past five days.
President Daniel arap Moi blamed Kenya's opposition, battling him for constitutional reforms ahead of elections due later this year, for the unrest, which has prompted the deployment of the army.
But a senior opposition politician, member of parliament Rashid Mzee, said he suspected Moi's ruling Kenya African National Union (KANU) was trying to sabotage the campaign for political reforms.
Provincial police chief Francis Gichuki, apparently unaware of Moi's remarks, told reporters in Mombasa that the clashes, which have raised the political temperature in Kenya, were mere thuggery.
Arsonists razed about 100 roadside kiosks and set fire to dozens of houses around Mombasa on Sunday after five Kenyans were killed and many hurt overnight by unidentified attackers, witnesses said.
"We are treating this as thuggery and do not see a political motive. The situation is fluid but it is under control. It took us by surprise," Gichuki said.

"So far we have arrested 69 people and they will appear in court from tomorrow. They are two politicians from Safina party and we are questioning them," he said, referring to the unregistered party headed by renowned conservationist Richard Leakey.
Opposition leaders said the Safina members had been held since Thursday, a day after attackers raided two police posts and killed six police officers.
The government sent in the army to back police and paramilitary units battling to end the violence and Gichuki said security forces using army aircraft had beefed up operations.
Police figures showed 31 people had been killed in the unrest and Gichuki said two local administrative police had gone missing but he gave no details.
Several thousand foreign tourists were advised to stay in their hotels on the coast north and south of Mombasa but officials said no visitors had been caught up in the violence.
Rsidents said those killed were mainly people who originally came from outside the coastal region. They pointed to leaflets, hand-written in Swahili, which had been distributed in the area.
"The time has come for us original inhabitants of the coast to claim what is rightly ours. We must remove these invaders from our land," the pamphlets said.
Karl-Heinz Straus, chairman of the Coastal Kenya Association of Tour Operators, said he feared that the violence could damage the tourism industry.
The leisure and tourism industry brought in around $465 million last year from 770,000 visitors, of whom more that half visited beaches in the Mombasa area.
